chapter.title: What is left: the owners' share

cards.body:
Picture the house again. It is worth 400,000 and the mortgage is 300,000. The 100,000 gap is yours. Where did it come from? Partly the deposit you paid in on day one, and partly the mortgage payments you have made since.

Equity on a balance sheet is that gap, and it has exactly two sources: money the owners put in, and profits the business kept instead of handing back.

cards.title: Two pots make up equity
cards.body:
Equity is what belongs to the owners after every debt is paid. It is the number that makes the sheet balance: assets minus liabilities.

On the sheet, equity is split into two pots. The first pot is money the owners put in when they bought shares. Companies call it share capital or paid-in capital. It is the deposit on the house.

The second pot is profit kept inside the business over the years. It is called retained earnings. Each year the company earns a profit, pays some of it out as dividends, and keeps the rest. The kept part is added to the pot.

So retained earnings is a running total, not one year's profit. A 20-year-old company has 20 years of kept profit stacked up in that line.

That is the whole idea. Equity is not cash sitting in a drawer. It is a record of where the owners' share came from.

cards.prompt: A company has made a profit every year for 10 years and paid out half of each year's profit as dividends. What happened to the other half?

options.text: It sits in the retained earnings line, added up over the 10 years
It was returned to the owners, so it is no longer on the balance sheet
It is counted as a liability, since the company owes it to shareholders

whyNot.b: That's the dividend half, not the kept half: the paid-out part leaves the sheet, the kept part stays in retained earnings.
whyNot.c: That's a debt, not equity: kept profit is not owed to anyone, it belongs to the owners already.

cards.reteach: Think of retained earnings as a jar. Each year the company drops in the profit it did not pay out as dividends. After 10 years the jar holds 10 years of kept profit. Nothing is owed on it; it is simply the owners' share growing.

cards.title: A bakery, three years in
cards.body:
Three friends start a bakery and each put in 20,000. Share capital is 60,000.

Year 1 profit is 15,000. They pay out 5,000 in dividends and keep 10,000. Retained earnings: 10,000.

Year 2 profit is 25,000. They pay out 10,000 and keep 15,000. Retained earnings: 25,000.

Year 3 is a loss of 8,000, with no dividend. Retained earnings fall to 17,000.

Equity at the end of year 3 is 60,000 plus 17,000, which is 77,000.

cards.title: When equity shrinks or turns negative
cards.body:
The bakery example shows the pot can go down. A loss year takes money out of retained earnings. A dividend bigger than that year's profit does the same.

If losses pile up long enough, retained earnings turn negative. Then the sheet calls them an accumulated deficit. If the deficit is bigger than share capital, total equity is negative. In the house picture, the mortgage is now bigger than the house.

A second surprise: equity is not what the company is worth. The balance sheet records assets at what they cost, less wear and tear, not what someone would pay today. A brand the company built itself is not on the sheet at all. So the market price of all the shares can be far above equity, or below it.

Equity tells you what the owners have put in and kept. It does not tell you what a buyer would pay.

cards.prompt: A company's balance sheet shows share capital of 50,000 and an accumulated deficit of 70,000. A friend says the business is clearly worth nothing. Which is the fair reading?

options.text: Equity is negative 20,000. Losses have eaten all the money put in and more, but the sheet does not say what a buyer would pay
Equity is 120,000, since both lines add to the owners' share
Equity is negative 20,000, so the shares must be worthless

whyNot.b: That's adding instead of subtracting: a deficit is kept losses, so it comes off share capital, not on top of it.
whyNot.c: That's mixing equity with market value: the sheet records costs, not what someone would pay, so negative equity is a warning, not a price.

cards.reteach: Start with what owners put in: 50,000. Take away the losses the company has stacked up: 70,000. The result is negative 20,000, so debts now exceed what the company owns on paper. That is a serious sign. But the sheet uses historic costs, so it is not a price tag.

cards.body:
The common slip is reading retained earnings as cash the company is holding. It is not. Kept profit was spent long ago on ovens, stock, or paying down loans.

To spot it: look at the cash line in assets. If retained earnings is 2 million and cash is 50,000, the profit was reinvested, not saved. Equity records where money came from, never where it is now.

cards.prompt: What are the two sources of equity on a balance sheet?

options.text: Money the owners put in, and profit the company kept over the years
Cash in the bank, and money customers still owe
Share capital, and the total of all past profits before dividends

whyNot.b: Those are assets, not equity: they are things the company owns, not a record of where the owners' share came from.
whyNot.c: That's profit before dividends: retained earnings only counts the part kept after paying owners out.

cards.reteach: Equity has two pots. The first is what shareholders paid in for their shares. The second is a running total of profit the company kept rather than paid out as dividends. Add them together and you have the owners' share.

cards.body: Search for any listed company's annual report, find the balance sheet, and locate the retained earnings line. Then compare it with the cash line. Say in one sentence whether kept profit was saved or reinvested.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain where the equity number came from, split it into money put in and profit kept, and say why it is not the company's price tag.
